activities.anchor: The circulatory system's three vessel types divide its labour
activities.caption: file each property under its vessel type
activities.name: phlVesselSort

config.prompt: Three vessel types, divided labour — file each property:

items.label: carry blood away from the heart under high pressure
microscopic exchange vessels, one cell thick
deliver oxygen and nutrients to tissue, collect waste
the draw of last resort — routine in newborns and point-of-care testing
return blood to the heart under low pressure through distensible walls
lie superficially, tolerate puncture and pressure, refill after the needle leaves

config.why: Arteries are avoided (they bleed vigorously and are hard to compress), capillaries are the fallback, and veins are the venipuncture target — which is why the whole map is venous.

activities.anchor: map is drawn on the antecubital fossa
activities.caption: build the vein preference order, first choice to refused
activities.name: phlVeinOrder

config.prompt: Assemble the site preference order, best first:
items: Median cubital — usually largest and best-anchored, and it sits away from the median nerve and brachial artery
Cephalic — runs along the thumb side of the forearm; often tender and prone to rolling
Basilic — little-finger side, closest to the median nerve and brachial artery; highest nerve-injury risk, extra care
Back of hand and wrist — smaller, more mobile veins, drawn with a smaller needle
Ankle and leg — generally avoided: clot and dependency problems, a physician-decision territory
config.why: Preference runs from safest anatomy down: the deeper the vein sits to nerve and artery, the later it comes — and some sites are refused outright.

activities.anchor: a vein is wherever you see something blue
activities.caption: pair what each finding under the finger means
activities.name: phlPalpateMatch

config.prompt: Sight misleads, touch decides — pair each finding with its verdict:

pairs.left: a firm, springy tube that rebounds
hard, and moves with finger motion
pairs.right: tendon — not a vessel at all

pairs.left: something that merely looks blue under the skin
pairs.right: sight misleads — veins palpate, they do not just look

config.why: Distinguishing vein from tendon and artery by feel is the skill — anatomy here is the difference between a routine draw and an injury claim.

activities.anchor: Spin a tube of blood and it separates
activities.caption: guess the magnitude — cells in a microlitre
activities.name: phlWbcEstimate

config.prompt: One microlitre of healthy blood holds roughly how many white blood cells (leukocytes)?
config.why: The healthy range runs about 4,000–11,000 per microlitre — the immune defenders. Red blood cells outnumber them spectacularly: several million per microlitre.
config.context: 4,000–11,000 leukocytes per microlitre vs several million erythrocytes — a factor of several hundred.

activities.anchor: each step has its safety logic
activities.caption: true or false — the procedure's safety logic
activities.name: phlProcJudge

statements.s: Tourniquet time should stay under a minute — prolonged tightening hemoconcentrates the blood and skews the results.
statements.why: Cells concentrate and fluid filters out, so a long tourniquet changes the very sample being drawn.

statements.s: Additive tubes are filled and then gently inverted to mix their additives.
statements.why: Gentle mixing spreads the additive; rough handling is a different failure mode (haemolysis) entirely.

statements.s: The tourniquet is released after the needle is withdrawn, to keep the vein full.
statements.why: It is released before needle withdrawal; pressure and gauze come after.

statements.s: An unlabelled specimen can be labelled back at the desk, as long as you remember the patient.
statements.why: 'Unlabelled specimen' means 'start again' — labels go on at the bedside, in the patient's presence, never pre-printed.

config.root: The requisition asks for a venous draw. The patient's right arm is the mastectomy side; the left forearm has an IV infusion running. Walk the call.

choices.label: Draw below the IV on the left arm
Draw above the IV on the left arm
Stop and consult rather than improvise

rightArm.text: A lifelong exclusion: lymph-node removal can leave that arm prone to lymphoedema and infection, and a puncture invites both.

below.text: Drawing below an infusion dilutes the sample with whatever is infusing — the specimen answers the drip, not the patient.

above.text: Drawing above it risks withdrawing the medication itself into your tube.

stop.text: The classic scenario: a mastectomy exclusion on one arm plus an IV on the other is exactly when the phlebotomist stops and consults rather than improvises.

config.why: Every exclusion site has a harm written into it — and when the exclusions cover both arms, the map itself says stop.

activities.anchor: the order of draw is bureaucratic convention
activities.caption: find the faulty step in this colleague's tube sequence
activities.name: phlDrawSpot

config.prompt: One step in this colleague's tube sequence is wrong — click it:
lines: Two spoken identifiers matched to the requisition; tourniquet on; median cubital selected.
First tube: light-blue citrate, filled to its exact nine-to-one ratio for the clotting tests.
Next: the red-top serum tube, drawn straight after the lavender EDTA tube.
Then the lavender EDTA tube for the complete blood count, gently inverted to mix.
Finally the grey fluoride tube for glucose — everything labelled at the bedside, in the patient's presence.
config.correction: The red-top tube must come before green and lavender: EDTA carryover from the lavender tube binds the chemistry sample's calcium invisibly and wrecks its potassium and calcium results.
config.why: The needle carries traces of each tube's additive into the next — the sequence (blood cultures, light blue, red/gold, green, lavender, grey) is chemistry law, not convention.

activities.anchor: When veins are not an option, the map moves to the capillaries
activities.caption: drag the divider — venous draw vs capillary draw
activities.name: phlCapCompare

config.prompt: One patient, two collection grammars — drag to compare:

before.label: venous draw
before.text: The default: antecubital veins, tubes filled to ratio, additives mixed by gentle inversion — and the reference ranges most laboratory tests assume.

after.label: capillary draw
after.text: Fingerstick (fleshy pad of the middle or ring finger) or warmed heelstick in newborns: wipe the first drop, no hard squeezing, microtainers filled in the same sequence. Results run slightly higher in haemoglobin and glucose — the laboratory's ranges must match the collection type.

config.why: Capillary sampling dominates where veins fail or volume is tiny: newborns (a venous draw would be a meaningful fraction of their total blood volume), inaccessible veins, and bedside point-of-care testing.
